#### exterior
*Now:* unchanged in sense 1; in sense 2 "exterior moments" is kept and now explained at 17m:70, while "zero-exterior-moment source" and "exterior discrepancy" are replaced (17m:155, 439).
*Variants:* exterior factors; exterior word; exterior separation; exterior insertions; exterior probes; exterior moments (17m); no longer in the text: zero-exterior-moment source, exterior discrepancy (17m).
1. **Outside the cluster.** Said of the insertions that do not belong to the cluster under study: the "exterior word" is the word of remaining insertions on which `A_w` / `B_h(w)` acts or against which a cluster is paired. In the source the exterior points are those kept away from the cluster and its centre by a distance that may itself tend to zero, more slowly than the size of the cluster; spectators are the special case of a fixed positive distance. v3 uses the distinction at 18:253–256 ("the replacement bound when exterior separation also tends to zero … Fixed-positive-clearance Proposition … by itself does not give that stronger result").
   *Basis:* S; I from the v3 text alone. *Where:* 13:338, 351, 368–384; 18lp:8, 154, 286, 294, 308, 323, 332 (18lp:207, 238 have "interior", the opposite word); 14:110; 15:246; 16:46, 70, 250; 18:254; 18r:10–12, 34, 37. *Proposed:* *exterior word* kept and defined once (the insertions outside the cluster, at distance from it large compared with its diameter); *spectator word* where the distance is fixed (14:729, 905; 14lc:43).
   *Source:* Scott `part2/J-section.tex:400`: "Suppose the cluster lies within `e^{−αT+o(T)}` of `o` … Exterior points are at distance at least `e^{−βT−o(T)}` from every cluster point and `o`, and mutually at least `e^{−υT−o(T)}` apart, where `0 ≤ β < α` and `υ ≥ β`"; `J-section.tex:730`: "The exterior word may have internal separations as small as `e^{−T}`, but it stays at distance at least `e^{−sT−o(T)}` from the cluster"; Scott `part1/02-definitions.tex:293`: "spectators `y` are `δ_sp`-clear if `|o − y_j| ≥ δ_sp` and `|y_j − y_{j'}| ≥ δ_sp`".
2. **Against outside spectators (17m).** "Exterior moments" of a source are its integrals against spectators independent of the varied coarse links: "its integral against every spectator independent of the varied coarse links is zero … not an assertion that a finite Taylor polynomial alone has zero exterior moments, that is, zero integral against every spectator independent of the varied links" (17m:67–70); "the full differentiated kernel, with zero exterior moments" (17m:155), "the full differentiated kernel with zero exterior moments" (17m:440). 17m:439 now reads "the normalized residual of (ch11:descent-error)".
   *Basis:* D (17m:70); R (17m:67–70). *Where:* 17m:70, 155, 440. *Proposed:* *integrals against spectators independent of the varied links* (now the gloss at 17m:70; the word is kept).
*Across chapters:* sense 1 in chapters 13–16 and 18, never defined in v3; sense 2 in 17m, explained in place; in 2e the former "exterior spectator" is now the *exterior function* (2e:41), a function of far links (see *exterior spectator*). The opposite word is "interior" (supported inside the cell). *Spectators* is kept, defined once, for insertions at fixed distance; the earlier proposal to replace "exterior word" by "spectator word" everywhere would erase the case of 18:253–256, where the exterior distance shrinks. "The exterior integrand" (9s:170) is an ordinary use (outside a region); 11R:267 now says "the corresponding action terms far from the large-field set". The standard "exterior derivative / multiplication" of chapters 5, 7 and 11 is not this word.
*See also:* exterior spectator; discrepancy (sense 5); spectator.

#### exterior row
*Now:* replaced by *the bounds for the corresponding action terms far from the large-field set* ("Indeed the bounds for the corresponding action terms far from the large-field set, and the local determinant and Haar bounds are `y^{−1/4+o(1)}`", 11R:267–268).
*Variants:* exterior ceiling charges (source only).
- **Meaning.** The terms of the action, after the Gaussian extraction, that are not assigned to any selected large-field component. To each elementary term ("row") of the fine action, of the block-average penalty and of the coarse counterterm belongs its energy, minus the affine square subtracted from it if the row is selected, plus its extracted mean square; a selected component is assigned the rows anchored within a fixed multiple of `B` of it (the energy `𝓔_O^rem` of (ch06:component-extracted-energy), 6:1431–1444), and the exterior rows are the remaining ones. In "the bounds for the corresponding action terms far from the large-field set, and the local determinant and Haar bounds are `y^{-1/4+o(1)}`" (11R:267–268, formerly "exterior row, determinant and Haar") the three items are three of the eight contributions to the unselected local exponent: these action terms, the local determinants outside the selected components, and the local Haar logarithm. In the table of 6:1253–1262 the first is the pair of lines "nonlinear action remainders far from `A`" and "extracted mean squares far from `A`"; the other two are presumably the lines "local determinant differences" and "local Haar logarithms" (by name only).
  *Basis:* S. The identification with the first two lines of the table of 6:1253–1258 no longer rests on position: the source defines the charge of a row by the rule which 6:1441–1444 states for the energy assigned to a component (see *Source*), so the exterior charges are the nonlinear remainders and mean squares of the rows outside the components. Not checked: that the bound `y^{-1/4+o(1)}` of 11R:267–268 is the chapter 6 bound evaluated at the recording parameter `y`. *Where:* 11R:267. *Adopted:* *the bounds for the action terms far from the large-field set, the local determinants and the Haar logarithm (table of Section ch06:primitive-bounds)*; 11R:267 does not cite the table.
  *Source:* Martin existence/actual-corrected-body-compiler.tex:93–98 ("The remaining term is the sum of eight specified contributions: exterior ceiling charges, the linear residual, the quadratic inverse correction, exterior local determinants, the relative logarithmic determinant series, its inverse-correction logarithmic series, the local Haar logarithm, and the inherited fine/coarse remainder"), :99–100 ("obtained by partitioning the ceiling charges into owner ceilings and their complement"), :137–139 ("Each exterior ceiling term is at most `4ω_𝒮 y^{-1/4}`"). The charge ("levy") of a row: existence/actual-harvested-owner-energy.tex:203–231 (`ω_𝒮 Σ_{j ∈ 𝒞_{200B}(O)} levy_j = Av_σ[𝒲_τ(anchor_{200B}(σO)) − 𝒳_{H_σ}(a_σ) + 𝒞_σ(m)]`; "Partition the oriented energy addresses into fine faces, predictor bonds, coarse faces and normalization rows … At a selected fine or predictor address the charged coordinate square equals the extracted affine square of the signed array … At an unselected address both subtracted terms are zero. The mean squares remain with the positive sign in the definition of the levy"), which is v3 6:1433–1444 term by term ("every near action term is assigned once; a retained fine curvature or averaging component subtracts its affine square; its extracted mean square is retained with positive sign. Components that are not retained subtract zero"); existence/actual-corrected-body-compiler.tex:298–299 (`ω_𝒮 Σ_j levy_j = M_0 + (R_f − e_0) − G_0(m + gZ) + G_0(m)`). No Lean declaration located.
*Across chapters:* one occurrence. "Row" was v3's word for the source's "oriented energy address" (v3 6:1441 now says "action term"; the source itself speaks of "the four row inventories", existence/actual-harvested-owner-energy.tex:238–240), and "exterior" is the complement of the regions assigned to the selected components ("partitioning the ceiling charges into owner ceilings and their complement"), for which chapter 6 now says "far from `A`" and 11R:267 "far from the large-field set". Why the source calls the term a "ceiling charge" was not traced.

The same object in role. In Bałaban's gauge papers the extraction is done by resumming over `X` and subtracting `β_j A` (see *affine Hessian*). ### F

#### `𝒰_F`
*Now:* replaced by *`W_F`* (as already noted below); the variants are replaced by "the fine field that the linearization of the critical configuration, in its representative `W_F` of (ch05:stationary-tangent), assigns to a coarse logarithmic field `h`" (6:960–961) and "the operator `W_F`" (6:979).
*Variants:* no longer in the text: stationary fine response (6:960); tree-straightened response (6:979).
- **Meaning.** A symbol that the text no longer contains: before 24 November 2026 the text had `𝒰_F`, undefined, at 6:960 and 6:983, where it now writes `W_F`. It denotes the linear map taking a coarse logarithmic field `h` to the fine stationary field in the tree (forest) coordinates: "Let `a = W_F h` be the fine field that the linearization of the critical configuration, in its representative `W_F` of (ch05:stationary-tangent), assigns to a coarse logarithmic field `h`" (6:960–961); "The operator `W_F` has a bounded row norm at fixed `L`: the exponentially decaying kernel of the linearization is summed absolutely, and the correction bringing it to the block axial gauge is a sum along finitely many tree edges per block. Thus the relative candidate `v = W_F h − rep h` is zero on the tree" (6:979–983). It is the forest representative `W_F` of the stationary tangent (5.stationary-tangent, 5:1149–1160): the smooth representative `W_a` plus the fine gradient that makes the result vanish on every tree link, with site potential zero at the block roots ("Finally adjust `W_a v` by the unique gradient `d_{0,f}φ` whose site potential is zero at every block root and makes all tree edges vanish", 5:1149–1153). The present text states the identification by writing `W_F` and now cites (ch05:stationary-tangent) at 6:960.
  *Basis:* R (6:960, 979–983) for the properties used and, in the present text, for the symbol `W_F`; S for the definition of `𝒰_F` and for its identification with `W_F`. *Where:* 6:960, 983 before 24 November 2026 (its only occurrences); none in the present text. *Adopted:* `W_F` at 6:960 and 6:983, as the text now has; add a reference to (5.stationary-tangent) (done at 6:960).
  *Source:* Martin `existence/local-mean.tex:11–27` "Write `𝒰_F b` for the fine stationary field in tree coordinates with coarse input `b`. It is the tree-straightened installed linear response. Its relative field is `v_F(b) = 𝒰_F b − b̄`, where `b̄` is the linear coarse replica. On every forest bond this difference is zero. … if `K_f, K_c` are the fine and coarse quadratic forms and `𝒬` is the rooted linear predictor, `K_c = 𝒰_F^* K_f 𝒰_F + p(1 − 𝒬𝒰_F)^*(1 − 𝒬𝒰_F)`". Lean, `YM/PREC/TreeMatch.lean`: `YM.Precision.straighten` and `YM.Precision.extracted S F W := W + d 0 f * straighten S F W` (definitions read); `YM.Precision.stays` (statement and proof read: `extracted S F W *ᵥ a` vanishes on every tree link); `YM.Precision.action` (statement and proof read: under `Inputs`, with `T = extracted S F W` and `P = 1 − probe S * T`, `Tᵀ * K H * T + penalty • (Pᵀ * P) = K H'`, which is Martin's display with `p` the penalty).
  Established: Martin defines `𝒰_F` in words as the tree-straightened linear response and gives its vanishing on the forest and the quadratic identity; the Lean operator `extracted` has exactly these two properties, and v3's `W_F` is defined at 5:1149–1152 by the same construction (a gradient correction making all tree edges vanish, zero at block roots). Inferred: that the three are one operator. No sentence of Martin or of v3 writes `𝒰_F = W_F`, and no Lean declaration carries either name; the identification is by agreement of the defining properties (same construction, same vanishing on the tree, same identities). The Lean matrices act on scalar one-forms and are applied colour component by colour component (`YM.Precision.relative`, `YM/PCalc/Chart.lean`, definition read). `audit/chapter-09-stationary-independent-review.md` (correction 2, not reopened) makes the same identification.
*Literature:* see *stationary tangent*.
*Across chapters:* chapter 6 only. The same operator is "the representative `W_F` in the block axial gauge" (9s:194; 6:954), "its representative in the block axial gauge is `W_F`" (7:583) and "the linearization `W` of the critical configuration, taken in its representative `W_F` in the block axial gauge" (11:642). It is not `W_a` and not `W_s`. 6:960 now points to the definition in chapter 5 instead of restating it.
*See also:* response (sense 4); stationary tangent; actual stationary tangent; forest.

*Variants:* the seven factor names of the table at 9:125–134, now "cubic remainder at the critical configuration", "centered determinant variation", "Haar remainder", "inherited quadratic-loop variation", "covariance and mean-equation residual", "incoming localized term", "large fluctuation-field event at a distinct event label"; no longer in the text: "stationary cubic remainder", "covariance and stationary residual".
- **Meaning.** Heading of the table of the elementary local factors of the block integral with their majorants (9:123–135). Each row is what is left of one term of the exponent after its leading part, which does not depend on the Gaussian variable or has already been assigned elsewhere, has been taken out: the action after its stationary quadratic part (the remainder then starts with the cubic Taylor term `β′(m_Y + gz)³`, 9:137–140); the determinant after its flat value and the quadratic term assigned to `α𝒬`; the Haar density after its value one and its vanishing first derivative at zero; the inherited loop action after its value at the mean. The rows correspond one to one to those of the source table, whose heading is simply "factor": cubic remainder at the critical configuration (formerly "stationary cubic remainder") = stationary-action remainder; centered determinant variation = centered determinant remainder; Haar remainder = Haar-Jacobian remainder; inherited quadratic-loop variation = inherited loop variation; covariance and mean-equation residual (formerly "covariance and stationary residual") = Gaussian-density and stationarity residuals; incoming localized term (formerly "incoming regular activity") = incoming regular sum; large fluctuation-field event at a distinct event label (formerly "cutoff failure at a distinct label") = cutoff remainder.
  *Basis:* R for the table (9:125–134); S for the subtractions row by row; ? for the former phrase, which occurs in neither source. *Where:* 9:125–134. *Proposed:* heading *factor* (as in the source) (adopted), with the subtraction stated in the sentence after the table for each row (not done).
  *Source:* Scott `part2/D-section.tex:149–160` (eq. D-factor-rates, columns "factor" and "integrated majorant"); `:162` "For the first row, Taylor's formula after the stationary quadratic part starts with `β′_u(m_Y + gz)³` … For the determinant, subtract its flat value and the quadratic term already assigned to `α_{N,m}𝒬_m`. The inverse identity bounds the remaining variation by `P_j(t_{m+1}+g)`. The covariance and sector mean-equation residuals are exponentially small … The chart density has value one and zero first derivative at zero, giving its quadratic bound. The inherited loop action is quadratic in slot curvatures … on the chart each slot is `O(t_{m+1} + g|z|)` and moves by `O(g|z|)`, which gives its row."
*Across chapters:* chapter 9 only. The words "after deterministic subtraction" were not found in Scott or Martin (searched for "deterministic"); they are present in the first v3 commit. Why the subtraction is called "deterministic" is not stated; the natural reading, that the subtracted parts are the values at the stationary (mean) configuration and do not involve the Gaussian variable, is an inference. v3 should restore Scott's two sentences on the determinant and the Haar density, which 9:141–143 compresses to "The other rows follow from the resolvent identity for the determinant, the second-order vanishing of the Haar correction, and the window errors".
*See also:* centered (sense 6).

#### field reconstruction
*Now:* not applied (18:69 still reads "define the unsymmetrized field reconstruction").
*Variants:* unsymmetrized field reconstruction `H_d(w)`; symmetric reconstruction `A_d w`, `B_d w`; reconstruction identity; reconstruction comparison.
- **Meaning.** (a) Unsymmetrized: `H_d(w) = Σ_{|α|≤d} b_α(w) u_α`, the field in `F_d` with the same values of the functionals `b_α`, `|α| ≤ d`, as the cluster word `w`, where `b_α(w)` is obtained by replacing the distinguished field in the probe correlations by the whole cluster (18:69–74). (b) Symmetric: `A_d w = ∫_{O(4)} R_d(K) H_d(K⁻¹w) dK`, the average of `H_d` over `O(4)`, and `B_d w = ½{A_d w + \overline{A_d w̄}}`, which is `A_d` made compatible with complex conjugation (18:83–86); 18:215 opposes "the unsymmetrized and symmetric reconstructions" without saying which of `A_d`, `B_d` is meant. The maps are defined for clusters all of whose rotations are clear of the probe points (18:77–80). Both maps fix every single field of degree at most `d` inserted at zero (18:88): writing `I_d A` for the one-letter word `A(0)`, `H_d ∘ I_d = id_{F_d}` (and `H_d(A(0)) = ι_{e,d}A` for `A ∈ F_e`, `e ≤ d`), so `H_d`, `A_d`, `B_d` are left inverses of the insertion `A ↦ A(0)` of a single field. On words they are not projections: a cluster word is not an element of a space containing `F_d`, so the maps are not endomorphisms. A projection appears only after composition with the insertion of a single field: on `F_t`, `t > D`, the map `A ↦ H_D(A(0))` is the low-degree component in the fixed biorthogonal system (18lp:276–278).
  *Basis:* D (18:69–71) for (a); D (18:83–86) for (b); R (18:88; 18lp:276–278) for "left inverse, not a projection". *Where:* 18:69, 83, 151, 215, 230, 231; 18r:7, 36 (8 of the 17 uses of "reconstruction" in ch. 17–19). *Proposed:* *the field in `F_d` with the same probe coordinates as the cluster `w`* (that is, the same values of the functionals `b_α`, `|α| ≤ d`); for (b), *its `O(4)`-average `A_d w`* and *`B_d w`*.
  *Source:* Scott `part2/J-section.tex:153–163`, Definition "Finite correlation projection" (`def:D31`): "Define the linear reconstruction map `D_j : ℂ^{𝒫_j} → F_j` … With `ev_j(A) = (S(A(0), B_{j,γ}))_γ`, it satisfies `D_j ev_j = id_{F_j}`: it is a fixed left inverse of field evaluation. For a word `w` separated from these probes, set `P_j^raw w = D_j((S(w, B_{j,γ}))_γ)`"; `J-section.tex:168–176`, Definition "Symmetric projection" (`def:D32`): `A_j w = ∫_{O(4)} R_j(h) P_j^raw(h⁻¹w) dh`, `B_j w = ½(A_j w + conj(A_j w̄))` "when every rotation of `w` is separated from every probe … Outside this domain set both maps to zero". So `H_d` is Scott's `P_d^raw`. Lean `YM.OPE.shadow` (`YM/OPE/Exchange/Coherence.lean:25`; definition read) `= Σ_{i ∈ bands} P.ope i x p o • P.loaded i d`, with `YM.OPE.Prescription.ope` (`YM/OPE/Splitting/Detector.lean:80`; definition read) the fixed finite combination of probe correlations of the word and `YM.OPE.Prescription.loaded` (`YM/OPE/Splitting/Basis.lean:49`; definition read) the basis field included in `F_d`; `YM.OPE.Prescription.SignedOff` (`Basis.lean:59–61`; definition read): biorthogonality `test_i(loaded_j) = δ_ij` and `Σ_i test_i(x) • loaded_i = x`; `YM.OPE.Orbits.old_fixes` (`YM/OPE/Orbits/Average.lean:55–56`; statement read): `shadow` of the one-letter word `v(0)`, `v ∈ F_d`, `d ≤ m`, equals the inclusion of `v` in `F_m`; `YM.OPE.Orbits.averageV` (`Average.lean:22`; definition read): the Haar average over `O(4)` if all rotations are clear of the probes, else `0`, with `average_fixes` (`Average.lean:66–67`; statement read); `YM.OPE.Orbits.checkReal` with `checkValue` (`YM/OPE/Orbits/Real.lean:37–43`; definition and statement read) `= ½(averageV(v) + conj(averageV(bar v)))`, with `checkReal_fixed` (`Real.lean:81–82`; statement read). Thus `H_d` = `shadow`, `A_d` = `averageV`, `B_d` = `checkReal`.
*Across chapters:* chapter 18 only (18 and 18r); distinct from the relativistic (word) reconstruction of chapter 16. The source calls these maps "projections" (Scott `def:D31`, `def:D32`) while stating the left-inverse property; v3 should restore the sentence "it is a fixed left inverse of field evaluation" at 18:88 and should not call the maps projections.
*See also:* reconstruction; cluster; word.

#### field word
*Now:* unchanged (now defined at 16:296: "a word is a finite ordered list of letters").
- **Meaning.** A finite ordered list of letters `(A,f)`, `A ∈ F`, `f ∈ 𝒮(ℝ⁴)`; the empty list is the empty word `1`, and concatenation is the product. "A letter is a pair `(A,f)` with `A ∈ F`, `f ∈ 𝒮(ℝ⁴)`; a word is a finite ordered list of letters" (16:296).
  *Basis:* D (16:296); S for the empty word and the product. *Where:* 16:296–298. *Adopted:* keep, define once.
  *Source:* Martin existence/reconstruction.tex:18–23: "A letter is a pair `a = (v,f) ∈ E × 𝒮`, and a word is a finite ordered list of letters. Let `J : E → E` be an antilinear involution, put `a^* = (Jv, f̄)`, and define the star of a word by reversing its order and starring each letter. The empty word is denoted by `1`. Concatenation is written without an intervening symbol."
*Across chapters:* chapter 16; one of the many uses of "word". The defining clause of the source is now at 16:296.
*See also:* finite difference word; letter; word (sense 2).

#### filter
*Now:* partly replaced by *symbol (of the averaging operators)* (sense 1: "the accumulated symbol of the averaging operators", 5:328; "The directional symbol", 5:334; 5:759, 762; 5:390 "symbol composition"; 17c:367 "the identity for the linear averaging operator"; 11:1736 "box-multiplier identities", after the "centered box multiplier" of 5:209); remains in the label `ch05:history-filter`; sense 2 kept (13:198, 213, 215).
*Variants:* link multiplier (5:335, new); no longer in the text: accumulated filter; directional filter; box filter (11:1736, now "box-multiplier identities").
1. **Symbol of the averaging operator.** The Fourier multiplier of the composed averaging maps; a "box filter" is the average over a block. The link factors are now named: "the multipliers `r_A` of the averages along the links, the *link multipliers*" (5:335).
   *Basis:* D (5:328–336). *Where:* 5:328–336, 759–763 ("symbol"); 11:1736–1745 ("box-multiplier"); 17c:367 ("linear averaging operator"). *Adopted:* *symbol of the averaging operator*; *box multiplier* at 11:1736 (chapter 5's "centered box multiplier").
2. **Filter of sets.** "The filter is generated by ordered tails" (13:215–216): the standard notion.
   *Basis:* R (13:215–216). *Where:* 13:198, 213, 215–216. 19:38 now reads "may be chosen on ordered tails" and no longer uses the word. *Proposed:* standard; keep.
*Literature:* no name; **`u_k(p) = ∏_μ (e^{ip_μ} − 1)/(L^k(e^{iηp_μ} − 1))`** in the **momentum representation** (B84a p. 23, (1.31): "we write them in momentum representation"). Sense 1 (the Fourier multiplier `ŵ_L(θ)` of the averaging map) is the same object for the scalar block average `Q'_k`, with cornered blocks (hence a phase) and `j = 1` only; the `k`-fold composite corresponds to v3's "accumulated filter". Suggested: *Fourier transform (symbol) of the averaging operator*, "Bałaban's `u_k(p)`"; drop "filter".
*Across chapters:* sense 1 formerly in chapters 5, 11, 17; it no longer stands in prose (grep), only in the label `ch05:history-filter` (5:332, cited at 5:355, 761); sense 2 is ordinary mathematical usage in chapter 13.

#### first crossing
*Now:* partly replaced on 25 November 2026 (sentence repair) by the definitions: "stop backwards from `n` at the first scale `n'<n` with `log(a_{n'}/a_n)≥(b+2)log H_n`, and then at the first scale `n''<n'` with `log(a_{n''}/a_{n'})≥10 log B_n`" (17w:31–33); "For a prescribed small radius, the first `n` with `r(n,α_0)` at most that radius, together with continuity of `r(n,u)` in `u`, places that radius in one of them" (17:138–139). Remains at 17m:422 ("is the first crossing") and 17m:429 ("at the first backward crossing"). The related "overshoot" is now "excess over the target" (17:142; 17w:36).
*Variants:* first backward crossing.
- **Meaning.** The first level at which a difference of `τ_m = log(1/a_m)` (10:146–147), that is the logarithm of a ratio of lattice spacings, reaches a target. Towards finer levels: "`τ_{k(n)} − τ_n ≥ T_n` is the first crossing" (17m:421–422; this is the `k(n)` of 17:108). Towards coarser levels: "Place a copy in each reflected cell at the first backward crossing of `B_n²`, so `B_n² ≤ a_m/a_n ≤ L_*B_n²`" (17m:429–430). At 17w:31 the crossing quantity is the accumulated logarithm of the block ratios below `n`, `Σ log L_i = log(a_m/a_n)`: one stops at the first `m < n` with `log(a_m/a_n) ≥ (b+2) log H_n`, and again at the first level a further `10 log B_n` below; the text now says this (17w:31–33). The "excess over the target" is the excess of that logarithm over the target (17w:36). At 17:138 (formerly "The first crossing places a prescribed radius in one of them") the crossing is of another kind: the first level `n` at which the decreasing sequence `r(n, α_0)` falls to the prescribed radius, as the text now says. The term is not defined at 17m:422, 429.
  *Basis:* R (17m:421, 429–430); R since 25 November 2026 at 17w:31–33 and 17:138 (S before). *Where:* 17m:422, 429 (the word); 17:138–139; 17w:31–33 (now written out); 17:142; 17w:36, 102, 105. *Adopted:* *the first scale `n'<n` with `log(a_{n'}/a_n) ≥ …`*, printed (17w:31–32; 17:138). *Proposed:* the same at 17m:422, 429 (not applied).
  *Source:* Scott `part2/I-section.tex:91`: "For each of the three exponents `b = α_j + u − α_0`, stop backwards from `n` when the accumulated logarithmic block length first exceeds `(b+2) log M_n`, then stop again after another `10 log B_n` … Each overshoot is therefore `O(log log β̂_n) = o(log M_n)`"; `I-section.tex:109`: "Monotonicity of `M_n` gives `r(n, α_0) ≤ r(n+1, α_0+1)`, while `r(n, α_0) → 0`. First crossing of any prescribed small radius, followed by continuity in `u`, puts that radius in one of these intervals."
*Across chapters:* chapter 17, resting on 10:146–147; the analogous choice of chapters 13 and 18lp is the *first-below scale*.
*See also:* first-below scale; overshoot.

#### fixed common coefficient functionals
*Now:* not applied; remains at 10:342, 376, 816, 892.
*Variants:* fixed linear coefficient functionals; coefficient functionals.
- **Meaning.** The fixed linear maps that assign to an action its array of path coefficients, used with one definition at every cutoff ("common"): "the linear curl division and the choice of coordinate contours of Chapter 7", fixed "once on the common index sets of the coefficients" (10:317–319) because "a representation by transported curvature terms is not unique" (10:316–319). Being linear, they carry the affine dependence of the outgoing cubic, quartic and loop terms on the incoming ones (10:335–341) over to the coefficient arrays: "Fixed linear coefficient functionals preserve these identities" (10:342). The alternative named at 10:319–322, the representative orthogonal to the kernel of all periodic Taylor coefficients inside the admissible subspace, is the choice made in the source manuscript, whose maps are the "readouts" `T_{m,q,p}`: array ↦ degree-`q` Taylor coefficient at zero of its path sum on the torus of the `p`-th period.
  *Basis:* R (10:316–319, 342) for the maps; I that "coefficient functionals" names exactly these maps (the phrase has no defining sentence), supported by the chapter audit note. *Where:* 10:342, 376, 816, 892. *Proposed:* *the fixed linear maps (curl division, choice of coordinate contours) that define the coefficient arrays*, named once at 10:316–319.
  *Source:* `audit/chapter-10.md`:10 ("Fixed linear curl division/readouts avoid arbitrary representatives"); Martin existence/background-path-convergence.tex:24–37 ("For each `p` let `T_{m,q,p}` be the continuous linear map which sends an array to the degree-`q` Taylor coefficient at zero of its path sum on the torus of side `n_m(p)` … `A^sel_{m,q} = A_{m,q} ∩ K_{m,q}^⊥` … Two selected arrays with the same readouts on every prescribed period are equal"); Scott part2/D-section.tex:1086 ("These are the degree extractions in Lemmas C4–C7"). No Lean declaration located.
*Across chapters:* chapter 10 only. Unrelated to the coefficient functionals `𝗾`, `𝗹`, `𝗵`, `𝖼` of chapter 17, which are explicit (see *Haar coefficient*).

#### fixed-input continuity
*Now:* not applied; remains at 11:1043; 12:36, 41, 129, 134–135, 142; 19:47.
*Variants:* fixed-input cutoff continuity; fixed-input comparison; fixed-input convergence (19:47–52).
1. **Continuity in the cutoff of the step with insertions at a fixed argument (ch. 12).** "At each fixed scale, applying the cutoff-dependent step with insertions to any fixed admissible remainder graph (Section ch12:graphs) gives Cauchy output graphs and coefficient maps. This condition is stronger than contraction for two graphs acted on by the same map."
   *Basis:* D (12:36–39). *Where:* 11:1043 ("including ball invariance and fixed-input continuity", before the definition); 12:36, 41, 129, 134, 142. *Proposed:* *continuity in the cutoff at fixed argument*.
   *Source:* Scott `part2/E-section.tex:685` (table row "marked steps on the two finite-cutoff histories"): "a common graph class and fixed-input convergence on a dense core are needed; see Lemmas `lem:E-common-core`–`lem:E-fixed-level`".
2. **"Fixed-input convergence" (19:47), credited to Chapters 9 and 10.** The corresponding statement for the unmarked step and its consequence: if the step maps of different cutoffs `N` are applied at a fixed level to inputs with common limits, the differences of the outputs tend to zero (last assertion of Proposition (10.stability-assumption), 10:445–450; called "common-input continuity" at 10:801 and "common-input cutoff comparison" at 10:841); hence the inverse couplings and activity arrays converge at each fixed level `m` and period index `p` as `N → ∞` (Theorem "Fixed-scale convergence" (10.convergence), 10:813–823).
   *Basis:* I (19:46–48 names Chapters 9 and 10; 10:445–450, 813–823). *Where:* 19:47. *Proposed:* *Proposition (10.stability-assumption) (last assertion) and Theorem (10.convergence)*, cited by number.
   *Source:* Scott `part2/D-section.tex:1077`, Lemma "Continuity in the cutoff" (`lem:D-cutoff-continuity`), and `D-section.tex:1202–1203`, Lemma "Fixed-level limits of couplings and activities" (`lem:D-fixed-level`): "For fixed `p,m`, the selected scalar couplings and activity coordinates … converge along every full cutoff sequence". Lean not searched.
*Across chapters:* the phrase is defined in chapter 12 for the marked step (sense 1). In chapter 19 it is a pointer by nickname; that it points to the chapter 10 statements (sense 2) and not to the chapter 12 one is inferred from the words "Chapters 9 and 10" at 19:46–47. v3 has three names for the chapter 10 statement (common-input continuity, common-input cutoff comparison, fixed-input convergence); cite it by number.
*See also:* graph.

#### fixed-position read
*Now:* replaced by *the link read at a fixed position* (sense 1, 7:646); *averaged link at a fixed position of the transporter* (sense 2, 7:719).
*Variants:* no longer in the text: fixed-position averaged read.
1. **The link at a fixed position of one straight piece of a coordinate path (7:646).** A coordinate path between two points `x, y` of the patch has four straight pieces, one per axis. For a fixed piece and a fixed position `k` along it, the link read is a function of the pair `(x,y)`: it is the link in the direction of that piece at the point obtained from the coordinatewise splice of `x` and `y` (the coordinates of `y` on the axes already traversed, those of `x` on the others) by `k` steps. "For the coordinate contours of the transporters, the link read at a fixed position sits at a translate of a point having some coordinates of each endpoint" (7:645–646); the exchange of the corresponding coordinates of `x` and `y` preserves the uniform measure on pairs, which is what lets the estimate for a single link be applied to the path.
   *Basis:* S. *Where:* 7:646. *Adopted:* *the link at a fixed position along one straight piece of the contour, as a function of the two endpoints*.
   *Source:* Martin `existence/weighted-frame-penalty.tex:78–83`: "Apply this on the enlarged block `𝓑` of radius `(J+3)L`. For pairs of endpoints, a coordinate path has four straight pieces, each of length at most `2(J+3)L`. At a fixed position along one piece, the link read is a translate of the coordinatewise splice of the two endpoints. Swapping the corresponding endpoint coordinates is a bijection of `𝓑×𝓑` and preserves its uniform measure." Lean declarations: see *coordinatewise splice*.
2. **The link at a fixed position of the straight connector, averaged over the offsets (7:719).** For the block average, the link at position `r`, `0 ≤ r < L`, of the straight connector of a coarse edge (now the "transporter", 4:186), averaged over the offsets `z` with the weights `w^av` (4:186–201): a linear functional of the fine field with coefficients `O_j(L^{-4})` on `O_j(L^4)` sites; the block average is the sum of the `L` of them ("each averaged link at a fixed position of the transporter has coefficients `O_j(L^{-4})` on `O_j(L^4)` sites, hence Euclidean row norm `O_j(L^{-2})`. Summing over its `L` positions along the transporter …", 7:719–722).
   *Basis:* R (7:719–722, with 4:186–201). *Where:* 7:719. *Adopted:* *the averaged link at a fixed position of the connector* (with "transporter" for "connector").
   *Source:* Martin `existence/weighted-stationary-inverses.tex:179–182`: "each fixed-position read has coefficients bounded by `C_J μ^4` on `O_J(L^4)` sites, hence Euclidean row norm at most `C'_J μ^2`; sum the `L` positions and use `h_l ≥ μ`."
*Across chapters:* chapter 7 only. In both uses a "read" is the value of one link, at a prescribed position of a path, regarded as a function of the remaining data (the endpoints in sense 1, the fine field after averaging in sense 2). The text at 7:646 says that the link "sits at a translate of" a point (the source: "the link read is a translate of the coordinatewise splice", the link being read at that point), but no longer names the coordinatewise splice.
*See also:* held fine reads; coordinatewise splice; padded block.

  *Basis:* I (17m:236–255). *Where:* 17m:251. *Proposed:* *choose `j` larger than the degrees of the finitely many polynomial fields used*; the text has the shorter "the order of the coefficient evaluations".
*Across chapters:* one occurrence. The proof of Proposition 17.spatial-moments has no counterpart in the source manuscripts, so the reading rests on the v3 context alone.
*See also:* probe.

#### flattening
*Now:* not applied; remains at 9:678.
- **Meaning.** Replacing a compatible family of new labels by the family of all their constituents: each new label is a connected component (in the graph of intersecting supports) consisting of old large-field labels and chosen correction labels (formerly "selected logarithmic labels", 9:673), and flattening forgets the grouping, giving one family of old large-field labels and one finite set of correction labels. It is the inverse of "taking components": "Conversely flattening a compatible family of new labels recovers the old disjoint covering family and the chosen correction labels. No constituent label is repeated …" (9:678–680).
  *Basis:* I (9:674–680); S for the statement that flattening and taking components are inverse to each other. *Where:* 9:678. *Proposed:* *replacing each new label by its constituent labels*.
  *Source:* Martin `existence/soft-log-fusion.tex:94–105`: "Conversely, take an admissible new family with nonzero product and flatten its labels. Within each component the old hard supports are disjoint by definition; between components they are disjoint because the whole component supports are disjoint. … Flattening therefore gives an admissible hard family and a finite set of logarithmic labels. No label is duplicated between components, because its support is nonempty and would otherwise meet both disjoint component supports. The connected components of the flattened support graph are exactly the original new labels. This proves that flattening and taking components are inverse on nonzero terms"; the same in `existence/forced-exclusion.tex:84–94`.
*Across chapters:* one occurrence; neither v3 nor the source defines the word in a sentence of its own, but the source's proof fixes its meaning (text read at 9:670–682).

#### fold
*Now:* partly replaced by *reflected periodic extension* (sense 2, 9s:174, 176, 238; the map is now "reflection map", 9s:180); remains at 7:820 (sense 1, "Folding the fine symbol into coarse momentum"), where nothing was applied.
*Variants:* no longer in the text: folded (auxiliary configuration, field); folding map.
1. **Pullback to coarse momentum (aliasing sum).** "Folding the fine symbol into coarse momentum also preserves `α`" (7:820): the quadratic kernel `Y` of a functional of the fine field is pulled back under the interpolation `W`, whose fine Fourier components at coarse momentum `ξ` are the alias amplitudes `N_z(ξ)` at the fine momenta `k_z = (ξ + 2πz)/L`; the result is the coarse symbol `L⁴ Σ_z N_{−z}(−ξ)^T Y(k_z) N_z(ξ)`, a sum over the aliases. The next sentences of v3 treat the nonzero and the zero alias of this sum (7:822–828).
   *Basis:* I (7:820–828); S for the formula. *Where:* 7:820. *Proposed:* *pullback to coarse momentum, a sum over aliases*.
   *Source:* Scott `part2/C-section.tex:237–241`: "Step 1: folding. … Let `N_z(ξ)` be the fine alias amplitudes of the rooted interpolation `W_0 = W_r`, at momenta `k_z = (ξ+2πz)/ℓ`. … With the Fourier kernels normalized per site, that kernel is `ℓ⁴ Σ_z N_{−z}(−ξ)^T Y_μ(k_z) N_z(ξ)`, where opposite aliases pair by fine translation invariance. … The factor `ℓ⁴` is the ratio of fine to coarse sites"; `:234` "We (1) fold `Π_μ` to coarse momentum, which leaves `α_b` unchanged".
2. **Reflected extension.** Pullback of the field under the reflection map `π_v(q) = min(q̄, 2v − q̄)`, applied coordinatewise; the map is given at 9:327–331 without a name.
   *Basis:* R (9:327–331). *Where:* 9s:174, 176 ("reflected periodic extension"), 175 ("reflection map"), 233, 296. *Adopted:* *reflected periodic extension*.
   *Source:* Martin `existence/five-period-localization.tex:11–22`: "fold the cyclic set `ℤ/(2w)ℤ` onto `{0,…,w}` by `π_w(q) = min(q̄, 2w − q̄)` … For a gauge field `U` on a larger torus and an anchor `o`, the folded field `Φ_{w,o}U` on the side-`2w` torus reads the link of `U` between `o + π_w(q)` and `o + π_w(q + e_μ)`; a reversed link is read as its inverse."
*Across chapters:* two unrelated uses, in chapters 7 and 9s. 9s now says "reflected periodic extension" and "reflection map", but 9:327–331 still gives the map without a name; it should name it there.

- **Meaning.** The degree-dependent subtraction over collision subsets ("subsets of coincident points" in the text, 18:402, 415), hence over forests of nested or disjoint subsets, that the text describes for a single shell at 18:401–413: for each collision subset `h`, with normal dimension `q_h = 4(|h| − 1)`, total input degree `d_h = Σ_{i∈h} d_i` and `L_h = max(0, d_h + 1 − q_h)`, "one subtracts the normal Taylor jet of the test function through order `L_h − 1 − q` when `q < L_h`", for each field degree `q` extracted from the cluster by a contact projection. For several nested collisions the prescription is the recursion over subsets `h` with `|h| ≥ 2`: `Π_h^punct = Σ_{π partition of h, |π| ≥ 2} Π_{b∈π} C_b^ct`, `C_h^ct = −Σ_{q<L_h} R_{h,q} Π_h^punct · Tay^⊥_{h, L_h−1−q}`, `Π_h^full = Π_h^punct + C_h^ct`, starting from `C_{{i}}^ct = A_i(x_i) ⊗ 1`, where `Tay^⊥_{h,k} f(x) = χ(x_h^⊥/s_*) Σ_{l≤k} (1/l!) D^l f(x − x_h^⊥)[x_h^⊥, …, x_h^⊥]` is the Taylor polynomial of order `k` in the directions normal to the diagonal `Δ_h`, cut off at a fixed length `s_*`, and `R_{h,q}` replaces the fields of `h` by their degree-`q` contact projection at the centroid; in nested terms the Taylor operator of the larger subset acts on the test function first (18:417–419). The v3 text reports it as the prescription of its source ("This explains the source prescription and its proposed sharper local-order bound", 18:414) and does not use it: "A one-shell estimate alone does not verify that stronger forest prescription. It is formalized but not used in the main result: we use the fully specified pair-weighted subtraction (ch18:subtraction), for which absolute convergence at all patterns of coincident points was proved directly" (18:421–424; until 25 November 2026 "We have therefore used the fully specified pair-weighted subtraction").
  *Basis:* R (18:401–414) for the one-shell rule; S for the nested recursion. *Where:* 18:401–422 (the words at 18:414, 422). *Proposed:* *the degree-dependent forest subtraction*, with its recursion displayed or cited; replace "source" by a citation.
  *Source:* Scott `part2/J-section.tex:647–670` (`eq:J-normal-Taylor`, `eq:J-contact-recursion`; quoted above); `J-section.tex:788–797`, Lemma "Contact extension and local order" (`lem:J2.2`): the normal subtractions "define a complex linear functional `𝔇` on `C_c^∞(ℝ^{4n})`" with `|𝔇(f)| ≤ C_K max_{|α| ≤ (W+2)n} ‖∂^α f‖_∞` and agreement with `∫ f S_n` on separated tests. Lean `YM.Contacts.Normal.System.degree`, `relative`, `depth`, `subtractAt`, `cumulant`, `punctured`, `full`, `full_formula` (`YM/Contacts/Score/Formula.lean:38–58`; definitions and statement read): `relative g = 4*(g.card−1)`; `depth g = degree g + 1 − relative g` (subtraction of natural numbers, so `max(0, ·)`); `subtractAt g F = −Σ_{w<depth g} reshape(reader g w) F * taylor (normalOn P g) s (depth g − 1 − w)`; `cumulant g` is the field `⊗ 1` if `g.card < 2` and otherwise `subtractAt g` applied to the sum over proper partitions of the cumulants of smaller subsets; `full g = punctured g + cumulant g`. `YM.Contacts.Normal.taylor`, `jet` (`YM/Contacts/Normal/Subtractions.lean:61–68`; definitions read) and `YM.Contacts.Normal.dimension_normal` (`YM/Contacts/Normal/Dimension.lean:50`; statement read): the normal space has dimension `4(g.card−1)`. This is the recursion above term by term. `YM.Contacts.Solstice.MultipleLight` (`YM/Contacts/Solstice/Result.lean:52–63`; definition read) has a field `distribution` with conclusion `Charge (majorKernel P g M t α o s) ⊤ (totalTestOrder d g)`, where `YM.Contacts.Solstice.totalTestOrder d g = (2 + Σ_j d_j) * g.card` (`YM/Contacts/Solstice/Skies.lean:48`; definition read) and `YM.Contacts.Solstice.Charge P U n` (`YM/Contacts/Solstice/Venue.lean:30–31`; definition read) bounds the pairing on each compact set by a constant times the `C^n` size of the test function; the theorem `YM.Contacts.Solstice.celestial` (`Result.lean:78`; statement read) states the existence of a family with `MultipleLight`; `YangMills.contactDistribution` (`ContactBridge.lean:14–17`; statement read) derives from `MultipleLight` the public statement `YangMills.Hierarchy.Contacts` (`ContactSpec.lean:12–14`; definition read), which records only the existence of a continuous linear functional agreeing with the correlation on separated test functions. Not opened: `majorKernel` (so the link between `distribution` and the recursion `full` was not traced), `Resolution`, `Sunshine`. The dependencies of the proof of `celestial` were not checked (no build, no `#print axioms`); a text search found no `sorry` and no `axiom` line in `YM/Contacts`, `YM/MultipleContact`.
*Across chapters:* chapter 18 only. The v3 statement that the prescription is not verified (18:421–424; `blueprint/notation.md:206`, "the unverified sharper source forest prescription") stands as the statement of the v3 text; since 25 November 2026 the text adds that it "is formalized but not used in the main result" (18:422), the author's description (decision 9), which the dictionary did not check against the formal source beyond what is recorded here. The Lean formalisation contains the recursion as a definition and a theorem statement with local order `(2 + Σ_j d_j)·n`, the order `(W+2)n` of Scott's lemma; whether that theorem depends on unproved assumptions was not checked, so this is a record of what is stated there, not a verification. v3 dropped the recursion for nested subsets; if the prescription is to be mentioned, v3 should restore Scott's display (`eq:J-contact-recursion`) with the sentence "expanding it gives forests of disjoint or nested collision subsets. This is a position-space forest formula" (Scott `part2/J-section.tex:677`).
*See also:* source prescription.

#### forgetting
*Now:* replaced on 25 November 2026 in the title of the proposition at 12:132 by "Independence of the graph at the ultraviolet cutoff" (the dictionary's proposal, with "ultraviolet" added); upstream's merge of 26 November 2026 brought its own title "Independence of the terminal graph in the cutoff limit", and the author's decision of the same day set "Cauchy convergence of the graphs at a fixed scale" (12:132) (grep). The word survives only in the label `ch12:forgetting`. The review of 25 November had objected that "Independence" claims more than the proposition, which proves decay like `2^{1−h}` of the effect of the replaced graph (`repairs-review.md`, item 1); the present title names the conclusion.
*Variants:* no longer in the text: "Forgetting the terminal graph" (title of a proposition, 12:132).
- **Meaning.** Loss of dependence on the graph supplied at the fine end. If the graph of the trajectory at level `m+h` is replaced by any fixed admissible graph and this is propagated down `h` steps, the result is within `2^{1−h}` of the level-`m` graph of the trajectory (12:140–144); hence the graphs at a fixed level are Cauchy in the cutoff `N` (12:134–137). The "terminal graph" of the title is the graph at the fine end of the history, whose last level is the cutoff `N` (the "terminal index" of the source); the proof replaces it at level `m+h`, and the bound uses only that any two admissible graphs are within 2. Two inputs are used and must be kept apart: the contraction (the one-step map halves distances between graphs) and the fixed-input continuity (for each fixed graph `H` the outputs `Φ_{m,N}H` are Cauchy in `N`); the second does not follow from the first.
  *Basis:* R for the statement (12:140–144); S for "terminal", with I for the last step: the source body, like v3, never uses the phrase "terminal graph", only "terminal index `N`", and the formal source has no object of that name. *Where:* formerly 12:132. *Adopted:* "Independence of the graph at the ultraviolet cutoff" (12:132, 25 November 2026), since 26 November 2026 "Cauchy convergence of the graphs at a fixed scale" (decision on titles); the reviewer's objection is recorded under *Now*. Not "initial" in the title, although the source proof itself speaks of "any initial graph difference".
  *Source:* Martin existence/fixed-rung-convergence.tex:92–125 (subsubsection with the same title): "Write `G_{m,N}` for the selected graph at scale `m` in the history with terminal index `N`"; "Retain the following precise local stability input: for every fixed admissible graph `H`, the graphs `Φ_{m,N}H` are Cauchy in the preceding 'within' relation … the contraction alone does not imply it"; "replace `G_{m+h,N}` by one fixed admissible graph and propagate it downward through `h` steps … The exact history recursion and the bound 2 on any initial graph difference imply `G_{m,N}` is within `2^{1−h}` of `V_{m,N}^{(h)}`". Lean (namespace `YM.MergeProof.Matric`): `Club`, YM/FullVolume/Mark/Nursery.lean (structure read: one step between two adjacent levels, with `flow : Gram → Gram`, the map `Φ`; `leanings P`, a linear equivalence of the coefficient space, the map `I_G`; `trail`: `Within P Q x → Within (flow P) (flow Q) (x/2)`, the contraction; `toward`: the coefficient maps of `P`, `Q` differ by at most `c·x`); `TwoFold P := ∀ t > 0, ∃ n, ∀ i ≥ n, ∀ j ≥ n, Within (P i) (P j) t`, same file (definition read: the Cauchy property of a sequence of graphs in the relation `Within`); `Ritzy`, same file (structure read: for every fixed graph `P`, `TwoFold (fun i => (Y' i).flow P)` and the same for the coefficient maps: the fixed-input continuity); `Gear`, YM/FullVolume/Mark/Sages.lean (structure read: each step family is `Ritzy`, and eventually in `n`, `W i n = (T i h n).flow (W (i+1) n)`: the history recursion); private `Gear.shawls` (statement and proof read: for every level `i` and every `d'` there is a Cauchy sequence `V` with `Within (W i n) (V n) (2·(1/2)^{d'})` eventually; `V` is obtained by applying `d'` steps to the constant sequence `W (i+d') 0`, and the base case uses `Gram.two`, any two graphs are within 2); `Gear.voyages` (statement read: `TwoFold (W i)`, the graphs of the history at level `i` are Cauchy in `n`); `Gram.Within`, YM/FullVolume/Mark/Booths.lean (definition read: `‖Q.g v − U.g v‖ ≤ a·r·‖v‖` for all `v`).
*Across chapters:* chapter 12 only; the word is also in the label `ch12:forgetting`. The former title was taken verbatim from the source. In the formal proof what is "forgotten" is the graph `W (i+d') n` at level `i+d'`, which is replaced by a graph independent of `n`; the index `n` is the cutoff.
*See also:* graph; terminal; fixed-input continuity.

#### free
*Now:* partly replaced by *non-tree* (links, bonds, edges, coordinates) at all cited lines; remains at 9s:38, 127 ("free fine coordinates", "free fine links"), 9f:909 ("free edges"), 11:1980, 1993, 2002 ("free links", for the axial gauge of a single torus), outside the lines the entry cited, and in the symbol `N_free` (9:57, 67–68).
*Variants:* free links, edges, coordinates (only at 9s:38, 127; 9f:909; 11:1980–2002); no longer in the text: free bonds.
- **Meaning.** The links not in the block trees. In the block axial gauge the tree links are set to the identity and are not variables; the non-tree links carry product Haar measure. They are of two kinds: the *active* ones, whose logarithms are the Gaussian integration variables, and the *frozen* ones `Y`, held fixed in the Gaussian calculation and integrated afterwards with Haar measure: "Fix the sector and the conditioning variables `Y`: the non-tree links that are held fixed in the Gaussian integral and integrated afterwards, called *frozen* below. … Tree links are not integration variables. *Active* coordinates, the integration variables, are logarithms (Lie-algebra coordinates) of the remaining non-tree links outside `A^{[10B]}`" (6:447–449); "non-tree bonds, and zero on tree bonds" (6:1383). There is still no defining sentence for "non-tree"; the word is self-explanatory against the trees of 5:919–921.
  *Basis:* R (6:447–449, 1383). *Where:* 5:921, 1171; 6:447, 448, 496, 594, 1383 (all "non-tree"); `N_free` at 9:66–69 (9:57 "`N_free` non-tree …"). *Adopted:* *non-tree links*.
  *Source:* Scott `part2/B-section.tex:583`: "Integration of these gauge variables reduces its integral to product Haar measure on free links … In exponential coordinates write this measure as `J_*^{n_e} ∏_e J(ψ_e) dψ`, with `J(0) = 1` and `n_e` the number of free links"; `:1047`: "The tree links equal 1 by the gauge choice … and are not variables; the frozen links are free links, held fixed in the Gaussian calculation and integrated afterwards with Haar measure. Active coordinates are the remaining free-edge logarithms in the complement of the selected radius-`10B` neighbourhoods"; `:1171`: "Nonactive free links are the frozen links `Y`".
*Literature:* no name; the variables **`B̃`**, "variables `B` restricted to the set of bonds `Λ̃ = Λ ∖ (∪_y Ax(y) ∪ ∪_c B(c)∩c)`", with `B = C B̃` (B85c p. 428: "We can parametrize this subspace … using part of the variables `B`, which we denote by `B̃`"). An analogue: Bałaban removes the axial (tree) bonds and also solves the hard constraint `Q_1B = 0` for one bond per coarse bond; v3's soft constraint removes nothing beyond the tree. Suggested: *non-tree links* stands; there is no literature name.
*Across chapters:* this sense was confined to chapters 5–6 and 9 (plus 9s, 9f and 11:1980–2002); where replaced, it no longer collides with "free field" of chapter 3, where "free" means "of the Maxwell theory" ("free image" and "free polynomial space" are now "on-shell polynomial space").
*See also:* forest; frozen; free image; active coordinates.

#### front-column
*Now:* replaced on 25 November 2026 (sentence repair), and on 26 November 2026 given its defining sentence and `D_k` (List 2, item 9, and the decision on `D_k` of that day): "At a fixed comparison scale `k` the one-step bounds for the coefficient of one transferred insertion (its `ℓ¹` norm at scale `m` is at most `C_{J(m+1)}L_m^d` times that at scale `m+1`, with the stage column bound `C_j` of Section (ch10:choices)), applied successively from the reference scale `r(d)` to `k`, give `‖u‖_1 ≤ D_k‖Au‖_1`, uniformly in `N,p`, with `D_k = a_k^d ∏_{m=r(d)}^{k−1} C_{J(m+1)}L_m^d`; the factor `a_k^d` undoes the dimensionful normalization of `Au`" (11:1349–1350). The word no longer occurs. A margin note at 11:1349 says that the one-step bound is not stated in v3 (it is proved in Scott `part2/E-one-mark.tex:27–33` and in Lean `YM.Work.G08.cone_step`) and that chapter 10 does not yet require of `C_j` what its derivation needs (merge-2026-11-26.md).
*Variants:* no longer in the text: front-column bound (11:1349); inverse front-column bounds.
- **Meaning.** The one-step bound `‖x_m‖_1 ≤ C_{m+1} L_m^d ‖x_{m+1}‖_1` for the level-`m` coefficient `x_m` of one transferred insertion, where `C_{m+1} ≥ 1` is the stage column constant; beside it stands the bound in the other direction, `‖x_{m+1}‖_1 ≤ C_{m+1}‖x_m‖_1`. Applying the first from the reference level up to level `k` and undoing the factor `a_k^{-d}` in `A` gives `‖u‖_1 ≤ D_k ‖Au‖_1` with `D_k = a_k^d ∏_{i<k} C_{i+1} L_i^d` (11:1349–1350).
  *Basis:* R since 26 November 2026 (11:1349–1350 state the one-step bound and `D_k`); S for the proof of the one-step bound. *Where:* 11:1349–1350. *Adopted:* *the one-step bounds for the coefficient of one transferred insertion*, with the inequality and `D_k` (26 November 2026; on 25 November only *the one-step coefficient bounds* had been adopted, because the constants were not defined in chapter 11). Not verifiable from the text, per the reviewer of 26 November: the constant and the normalization in `D_k`; whether the earlier `C_k` at 11:1166 is `C_{J(k)}` (as the margin note at 11:1349 says) or `C_{J(k+1)}`.
  *Source:* Martin existence/actual-rank-purchases.tex:176–188 ("`|v|_1 ≤ D_k|A_{k,N,p}v|_1`. Explicitly one may take `D_k = a_k^d ∏_{u=0}^{k-1} C_{u+1}L_u^d`, where `C_{u+1} ≥ 1` is the purchased front-column bound"). Lean `YM.Source.TransferData.Based.front`, `.back` (YM/Source/Insertion.lean:93–98; fields of the structure, read), `YM.RG.Stage.columns`, `.columns_ge` (YM/RG/History.lean:53, 60; read), `YM.Next.Rank.Price.outward`, `.at_current`, `.reference_size`, `.awake` (YM/Next/RANK/Matrices.lean:26–61; definitions and statements read).
*Across chapters:* one occurrence. The misleading word "inverse", which was not in the source, is no longer in v3: what is used is the front bound itself (it bounds the inverse of the transfer of coefficients). The Lean product `outward` and the source's `D_k` agree factor by factor.
*See also:* column.

#### frozen
*Now:* partly replaced by *conditioning variables* (sense 1, at its definition, 6:447, which keeps "frozen" as the working name: "called *frozen* below"); *held constant* (sense 2, 7:743–747; 11R:247). "Frozen" remains in sense 1 at 25 lines of chapter 6, at 9:73, 926 and at 9f:935 ("frozen coordinate").
*Variants:* frozen links; frozen logarithms; frozen inverse coupling; no longer in the text: frozen weights (now "constant weights", 7:744).
1. **Links held fixed in the Gaussian integral.** The non-tree links near the large-field set, held fixed in the Gaussian integral and integrated afterwards: "Fix the sector and the conditioning variables `Y`: the non-tree links that are held fixed in the Gaussian integral and integrated afterwards, called *frozen* below" (6:447), followed by a remark crediting the word "conditioning" to Bałaban and stating that here the integrations are carried out in the same step.
   *Basis:* D (6:447). *Where:* 6:447 and 24 more; 9:51, 58, 72–73, 926. *Proposed:* *conditioning variables*; introduced at 6:447 only.
2. **Held at a fixed value.** Weights held at their value at a real base point, against "moving" weights ("hold `h_l` constant", "these constant weights", 7:743–747); the inverse coupling held constant below the comparison scale ("Only the inverse coupling is held constant", 11R:247).
   *Basis:* R (7:743–746; 11R:247). *Where:* 7:743–747; 11R:247. *Adopted:* *held constant*.
*Literature:* **conditioning**; variables whose integrations are "left"; "spectator variables" (B85e p. 258: "We fix a configuration U = V_0 on Ω_1^c and we look for critical points of the functional"; B88a p. 12: "The integrals above are represented … as conditioning on Z_0^c"; p. 1: "integrals conditioned to subdomains of the lattice"; B88b p. 252 "conditional integral"; p. 256: "In the first step the integration with respect to the variables `U|_{Ω_1^c} = V_0` was left unchanged. Similarly in the next steps there are integrations with respect to variables on large field regions left"; D2 p. 092301-3: "Pieces of the action which are strictly localized in a large field region at some stage are not processed further"; p. 092301-61: "spectator variables left over from the early stages of the expansion"). An analogue of sense 1 with a real difference: v3 integrates the frozen links in the same step, by Haar measure; Bałaban carries them unintegrated inside `T_k` to later steps, until the R operation. Suggested: *conditioning variables* (Bałaban's word, B88a p. 12), with "Bałaban does not integrate them at that step"; not "spectator variables", which v3 uses for another object.
*Across chapters:* sense 1 in chapters 6 and 9; sense 2 in chapters 7 and 11R (text read at 6:446–449, 7:743–746, 11R:247–249), where the word "frozen" no longer occurs.
*See also:* free; history.

#### gain
*Now:* not applied; "gain" stands as before (21 occurrences); only "per-label gain" became "gain per term" (9:222).
*Variants:* gains; no longer in the text: per-label gain.
- **Meaning.** Improvement of a bound by a small factor ("the gain per term is `L^{-5}`", 9:222); the opposite of "loss".
  *Basis:* I. *Where:* 1:454; 2:391; 7:1056, 1166; 9:222, 246, 261, 265, 283 (9 uses); ch. 10 (1), ch. 11 (3) (examples for gain and loss together: 10:600; 11:502, 724; 11R:58, 144, 179); 17c:353, 363, 368, 380; 17m:132, 187, 330; 18:259. *Proposed:* *improves by a factor*; print the inequality.
*Literature:* **small factor**, **tiny factor**; "extract a factor"; "gain a tiny factor" (D1 p. 1330010-18: "If one of these conditions fails then we gain a tiny factor"; D3 p. 2154: "using the large field constraints to extract small factors"; §3.3 "Small Factors"; B85e p. 258; B88a p. 18: "We extract the expression α_6 exp(−δκ d_k(Y)) from each factor"; p. 16: "We use the first exponential factor in (2.19) to bound the sum"). The same informal usage for the verb "gain" and for "small factor". For the accounting nouns as such (cost, gain, loss, margin) B87, B88a, B85e and B88b–B89b have none: the operations are described by verbs ("controls", "is suppressed by", "can be made arbitrarily small"). Both observations hold: the usage exists as a verb and as "small factor", not as a system of nouns. Suggested: *small factor* for the large-field gain; otherwise print the inequality.
*Across chapters:* one sense; an accounting word, as in chapters 3–6.

#### gas
*Now:* not applied; "gas" stands (18 occurrences). Only the qualifiers changed: "ordinary gas" is now "polymer gas" (9:151), "unmarked gas" is now "the sum over disjoint covering families of the density without insertions" (18lp:186), and "exact-cover gas" is "sum over disjoint covering families" (decision of 26 November 2026).
*Variants:* polymer gas; no longer in the text: exact-cover gas; ordinary gas; unmarked gas.
- **Meaning.** A polymer sum: a sum over compatible families of products of activities. The "polymer gas without large-field sites" (9:151), formerly the "ordinary gas", has the activities that chapter 8 now calls "polymer activities" (`z_γ`, 8:288); the former "exact-cover gas", now the "sum over disjoint covering families", is the sum over disjoint covering families of products of large-field activities (12:181–183; `ℱ⁰` at 9:595), one factor of the density and equal to 1 when there is no large-field site; "the sum over disjoint covering families of the density without insertions" (18lp:186) is this factor for the density without source variables.
  *Basis:* R (9:151; 12:181–183; 18lp:186). *Where:* 8:288; 9:151, 154 ("small-field polymers"), 172 ("small-field factor"), 593; 12:181; 18lp:186. *Proposed:* *polymer sum*; *small-field polymer gas*; *large-field polymer sum over exact covers*.
  *Source:* Lean `YM.RG.Activities.gas`, `Activities.admissible`, YM/RG/Activities.lean (definitions read); `YM.RG.Rep.eval`, YM/RG/History.lean (definition read). Martin existence/terminal-marked-construction.tex:127–142 ("the unmarked density of the terminal representation", "the unmarked gas"). Details under *exact-cover gas* and *unmarked gas*.
*Literature:* **polymer expansion**; **exponentiated cluster expansion**; "Mayer expansion of the action density" (B88a p. 1: "the exponentiated cluster expansion"; p. 11: "The first step is the Mayer expansion of the action density"; p. 14, (2.12), (2.13)). The object (the polymer partition function `Z_pol(z)` and its logarithm) is the same, standard one. On the word two statements were made, "same object" (B88a) and "no counterpart" (D1, where the passage is direct from `∫exp(ΣH(X))dμ` to `exp(ΣH^#(Y))`, p. 1330010-38: "The cluster expansion gives this a local structure"); they agree: the object is in the literature, the word "gas" is in none of the papers read. For the exact-cover gas see *exact cover*. Suggested: *polymer sum* or *polymer expansion*; "gas" kept only if defined.
*Across chapters:* one notion with three qualifiers. The gas is a function of the configuration, one factor of the density; it must not be rendered as *partition function* or *density* (12:173–184).
*See also:* exact-cover gas; unmarked gas.

#### gauge completion
*Now:* replaced by *gauge-fixing term* (7:234, 321) and *gauge-fixed* inverse, operator, inverse propagator, Hessian (7:378, 887, 945, 1038; 17:248; 17t:89; 17c:145, 171, 177, 301); "completed" remains at 7:783 ("the blocked completed matrix `C_0`") and at 11:1696 ("the completed inverse", the inverse of `X^*HX + UU^*` in 11:1693, a completion of the same kind in chapter 11, not classified by the entry); the "completed fine kinetic matrix" of 17c:65 was removed on 25 November 2026.
*Variants:* completed (7:783; 11:1696); no longer in the text: completed inverse `𝒞^{-1}` (now "gauge-fixed inverse"); completed Hessian.
- **Meaning.** Adding `F*F` for a gauge condition `F` (or `d_U d_U*`) to a gauge-degenerate Hessian: "Given a gauge condition `F` with invertible `G = Fℛ`, put `C = 𝖩 + F*F`", where `𝖩` is the joint Hessian of 7:247. The gauge-fixed inverse is `𝒞^{-1} = (ℋ + F*F)^{-1}` (7:887–889).
  *Basis:* R (7:256–257). *Where:* 7:234 (title), 251–252, 313–314, 371, 879, 935, 1025; 17t:89–90. *Adopted:* *gauge-fixing term* for the added `F*F` (or `d_U d_U*`); *gauge-fixed operator* for the completed operator (`C = 𝖩 + F*F`; at zero field `H + dd*`, the operator of the Feynman gauge). Not for the block-completed form.
*Literature:* **gauge fixing term**, **gauge fixing density**; **Feynman gauge** (adding `‖∂*A‖²`) and **Landau gauge** (`δ_R(R∂*A)`, `R` a projection), obtained by the **Faddeev–Popov procedure**; the result is `Δ_a = ∂*∂ + ∂R∂* + aQ*Q = Δ − ∂P∂* + aQ*Q`, `Δ = ∂*∂ + ∂∂*` (B84a p. 20: "the best gauge from the point of view of regularity properties of Green's functions is the Feynman gauge. We will introduce a similar gauge for the lattice theory using the Faddeev–Popov procedure"; p. 24: "The gauge fixing density has the form"; p. 26; p. 29, (1.69); B87 p. 255: "we apply the usual Faddeev-Popov procedure"; p. 265: "the gauge transformation u_k … changing the axial gauge into the Landau gauge"). The same object for `H + dd*` at zero field, which is Bałaban's `Δ` (Feynman gauge); an analogue for `C = 𝖩 + F*F`, since Bałaban's gauge term is `∂R∂*` with the projection `R` onto `ΔN(Q'_k)`. Whether v3's gauge condition `F` of chapter 7 is of Landau type was not checked. Adopted (23 November 2026): *gauge-fixing term*; the completed operator is the *gauge-fixed operator* (Feynman gauge at zero field, Bałaban's `Δ`), in place of *gauge-fixed Hessian*; cite the Faddeev–Popov procedure. Not for the block-completed form. Whether the gauge condition `F` of chapter 7 is of Landau type remains unchecked, so `C = 𝖩 + F*F` is only an analogue of Bałaban's operator.
*Across chapters:* the same kind of completion in chapters 7 and 17, applied to different operators: 17t:89–90 has `H + dd*`, whose inverse is not the `𝒞^{-1}` of chapter 7; the "completed fine kinetic matrix" of the former 17c:65 was not traced before it was removed. Distinct from the block completion of 7:696–700 (now "the kinetic form with the penalty term added, the form `𝒢` below", still gauge-degenerate) and from the "positive completion" of chapters 3–6.
*See also:* exchange term; finite covariant path completion.

#### graded quotient comparison
*Now:* not applied; remains at 18:178.
- **Meaning.** A nickname (18:178, beside "the estimate (ch18:signed-transport)", formerly "the signed local transport", and "the stronger anchored marked support bound") for Proposition "Graded quotient estimate" (18.graded-estimate), 18gq:36–49: for `0 ≤ i ≤ t` there are constants `C_{t,i}(m)` with `log C_{t,i}(m) = o(τ_m)` such that, if labels `v_{N,p} ∈ V_t` converge to `v` on an ordered cutoff and volume refinement and `|x_m(v_{N,p})|_1 ≤ ε` there, then `dist_{F_t}([v], ι_{i−1,t} F_{i−1}) ≤ C_{t,i}(m) a_m^{−(t−i)} ε` (18.graded-distance). A label that is small at level `m` is, in the field space `F_t = V_t/N_t`, within `a_m^{−(t−i)}` times its size of the fields of degree below `i`, up to factors growing more slowly than any power of `a_m^{-1}`.
  *Basis:* R (18gq:36–49) for the estimate; I for the identification of the nickname with it (18:178 gives no reference; the proposition has the title "Graded quotient estimate"). *Where:* 18:178. *Proposed:* *the estimate (18.graded-distance)*, cited by number.
  *Source:* Scott `part2/J-section.tex:95–103`, Lemma "Graded quotient bound" (`lem:J-graded-quotient`), display (`eq:J-graded-input`): `dist_{F_t}([v], ȷ_{i−1,t} F_{i−1}) ≤ C_{t,i}(m) a_m^{−(t−i)} ε_bd`; "A label that is small at level `m` is therefore, in the quotient and up to subpower factors, within `a_m^{−(t−i)}` times its size of the fields of degree below `i`." `audit/chapter-18.md:10` lists `lem:J-graded-quotient` among the inputs of the chapter. Lean not searched.
*Across chapters:* single occurrence of the nickname.
*See also:* physical inclusion; signed local transport; anchored marked support bound.

#### graph
*Now:* unchanged; the explaining sentence proposed for sense 1 now stands at 11:380. In sense 2 "stationary graph" is replaced by *critical-configuration map* (10:925–927).
*Variants:* admissible graph; remainder graph; incoming / outgoing / output graph; graph at the ultraviolet cutoff (12:132 from 25 to 26 November 2026, formerly "terminal graph"; the title is now "Cauchy convergence of the graphs at a fixed scale"); selected graph; graph contraction; one-insertion graph estimates / contraction; coefficient graph (11:380, 468); no longer in the text: descending graph (now "the graph of the backward comparison", 17m:441).
1. **Linear map from coefficients to remainders.** A linear map `G : V_d → 𝓡_m` from the coefficient space of the labels of degree `d` to the normed space of remainder arrays at level `m` (regular and large-field remainders with their supports fixed); admissible when `‖Gx‖ ≤ s_m ‖x‖_1`. It assigns to each coefficient vector the remainder accompanying it, so that the density with one insertion at level `m` is described by the pairs `(x, Gx)`: this set is the graph of `G` over the coefficient space, whence the name. One marked step gives a coefficient map and a remainder map (`M_G`, `R_G` in chapter 11; `I_G`, `J_G` in chapter 12), and the outgoing graph is `G' = R_G M_G^{-1}`, `ΦG = J_G I_G^{-1}`; the map `G ↦ ΦG` halves the distance between two admissible graphs ("Graph contraction", 12:95). "Let `G` be an incoming linear graph of regular vanishing-jet and large-field remainders, with norm at most `s_f` per coefficient" (11:379–380).
   *Basis:* D for the bound (12:82–83); R for linearity (11:379–382) and for the reason of the name (11:380). *Where:* 11:347 (title), 379–382, 447, 911; 12:37–39, 82, 89, 92, 95 (17 occurrences in chapter 12); 17m:441; 18:126. *Adopted:* keep *graph*, with one explaining sentence taken from the source; 11:380 now reads "As in the graph transform for invariant manifolds, the step with insertions maps coefficient graphs at the fine scale to graphs at the coarse scale and halves the distance between two of them"; *graph transform* for `G ↦ ΦG` (11:468).
   *Source:* Scott part2/E-section.tex:242 ("A coefficient graph at level `m` is a linear choice `x ↦ g_m(x) = (R(x), Q(x))` of such remainders, with the supports fixed and `‖g_m(x)‖_rem ≤ C^col_{J_m}|x°|_1`. As in the graph transform for invariant manifolds, the marked step maps coefficient graphs at level `m+1` to graphs at level `m` and halves the distance between two of them"); Scott part2/E-one-mark.tex:100, 102 ("Define the new graph by `g_m(u) = g̃_m(M_m^{-1}u)`"; "This is the graph contraction"). Martin existence/fixed-rung-convergence.tex:33–50, 88 ("Represent a linear family of remainders by a map `G : F_d → E_m` with `‖Gv‖_{E_m} ≤ s_m‖core v‖_1`, `s_m ≥ 1`"; "any two allowed graphs are within 2"; "One step produces from `G` a coarse graph `ΦG` and an invertible coefficient map `I_G` … write its remainder map as `J_G = (ΦG)I_G`"; "the coarse graphs are within `a/2`"); this file uses "graph" as its noun for the map `G` and does not mention the graph transform. Lean `YM.MergeProof.Matric.Gram` (YM/FullVolume/Mark/Hinge.lean:12; structure read: `g : F.Coeff →ₗ[ℂ] Coin F Y c` with `‖g v‖ ≤ a · coeffSize (core v)`), `Gram.index`, `Gram.recorded`, `Gram.step` (Hinge.lean:45–56; definitions read: `step.g = recorded ∘ index⁻¹`), `Gram.Within` (YM/FullVolume/Mark/Booths.lean:40; definition read), `Gram.two` (YM/FullVolume/Mark/Prism.lean:19; statement read), `Gram.revenue` (Booths.lean:74; statement read: `Q.Within U t → (Q.step).Within (U.step) (t/2)`). The remainder space `Coin` and `F.core` were not unfolded. In chapter 11 the same object appears as `YM.Source.TransferData.entries` with `Based.linear` and `Based.cap` (YM/Source/Insertion.lean:72, 91–101; read).
2. **Ordinary senses.** "Intersection graph" (11:249); formerly "stationary graph" (10:925–927), the graph of the stationary map, now "critical-configuration map".
   *Basis:* R. *Where:* 11:249; 10:925–927 ("critical-configuration map"). *Proposed:* standard; keep.
*Across chapters:* sense 1 is the same object in chapters 11, 12, 17 and 18. Text read: 11:379–382, 11:446–448 and 12:82–95 gloss it, so "one-insertion graph contraction" (18:126) is the estimate of 11:347 ff. and the lemma "Graph contraction" (12:95), and "the graph of the backward comparison" (17m:441, formerly "descending graph") is that graph carried through the backward comparison of 11:893–920 (this last identification inferred). The two source manuscripts differ on one point: Scott's text names the graph transform of invariant-manifold theory as the model (E-section.tex:242), Martin's text does not; the comparison is therefore the source's own and not only general knowledge. v3 now has Scott's sentence at 11:380. In the former title "Forgetting the terminal graph" (12:132; from 25 November 2026 "Independence of the graph at the ultraviolet cutoff", since 26 November 2026 "Cauchy convergence of the graphs at a fixed scale") the graphs are the selected graphs `G_{m,N}` "at scale `m` in the history with terminal index `N`" (Martin existence/fixed-rung-convergence.tex:92–94, same title); the proof replaces `G_{m+h,N}` by one fixed admissible graph and finds `G_{m,N}` within `2^{1−h}` of the result (:114–121), so what is forgotten is the graph put in at the fine end `m+h`, and the conclusion is that `G_{m,N}` is Cauchy in the terminal index `N`. The source does not gloss the title either; Lean `YM.MergeProof.Matric.Gear` and `Gear.voyages` (YM/FullVolume/Mark/Sages.lean:14, 33; structure and statement read; `TwoFold` not unfolded). Not *remainder map*: the text uses that phrase for `R_G` (11:381–382) and `J_G` (12:90–92).
*See also:* fixed-input continuity; forgetting; linear graph.

#### group-coordinate contact identity
*Now:* replaced by *contact identity in group coordinates* (decision of 26 November 2026: subsection title 17t:178 "A contact identity in group coordinates"; 17t:499 "The contact identity in group coordinates"); "the group-coordinate identity" remains at 17t:174 (grep). The proposed title "An integration-by-parts identity in group coordinates" was applied and withdrawn the same day: Proposition (ch17:contact-identity) and its proof use the chain rule and a resolvent identity and no integration (merge-2026-11-26.md).
*Variants:* contact identity in group coordinates; contact identity; exact contact identity (17t:232, 336, 427); (17.contact); no longer in the text: group-coordinate contact identity.
- **Meaning.** The identity of the proposition at 17t:232–240, `½ tr(R D²(DS[Y])) − div_Haar Y = DΓ[Y] − μ² tr(RV) + DS[Z]`, an algebraic identity in the left-exponential coordinates `z ↦ e^z U` of the link groups ("group-coordinate"). It is unrelated to the contact (coincident-point) terms of chapters 18–19. The word "contact" is the one chapter 7 uses for the same kind of term (7:509 ff.): there the "contact term" is the gradient of the block penalty paired with the second derivative of the block average; here `DS[Z]` and `C_{ij} = DS[D_z² 𝒴_U(0)[e_i, e_j]]` (17t:222–228, 249–250) are the gradient of the action paired with the second derivative of the chart velocity. Why such a term is called "contact" is not explained in v3 or in its sources.
  *Basis:* D for the object (17t:232–240); S for the correspondence with chapter 7; ? for the reason for the word. *Where:* 17t:174, 178, 232, 336, 417, 427, 499, 503. *Proposed:* keep, cited by proposition number, with a remark that it is not a coincident-point term; the text has, since 26 November 2026, *contact identity in group coordinates*.
  *Source:* Scott `part2/I-section.tex:228–231` (the same identity, label `eq:I-contact`, with `Z = ½ contr(𝓡_μ, D²𝒴_U(0)) − contr(𝓖_μ d*(𝓥 + 𝓥*)𝓡_μ, 𝓙_U)`; no prose name); Martin `existence/thermal-contact-cancellation.tex:126–141` ("The finite-volume contact identity … It separates the pullback of the penalty Hessian from the gradient of the penalty paired with the second derivative of its constraint").
*Across chapters:* chapter 17 only. The common origin with chapter 7 is now read off the source of chapter 7; that the author of the chapter 17 label had it in mind is an inference from the equal structure of the two identities.
*See also:* contact (senses 2, 3).

### H

#### Haar-ball normalization argument
*Now:* replaced by *the lower bound for the partition function* (13sb:36) and, on 25 November 2026 (sentence repair of 10:172–175), by "the lower bound on the partition function from the Haar measure of a small ball about the identity on every link, as in (ch11:replicated-bound)" (10:172–173). The phrase no longer occurs in the chapter files.
*Variants:* no longer in the text: the Haar-ball argument; Haar-ball normalization (10:172).
- **Meaning.** The lower bound for the partition function obtained by restricting every link to a small ball around the identity: by a packing argument and Haar invariance `μ_G{χ(U) ≤ r} ≥ (r/4)^{D_G}`, so the event that every forward link is within `ρ/4` of the identity has probability at least `(ρ/16)^{4D_GV}`, on it the large-field indicators vanish and the action is bounded, and positivity gives `Z ≥ exp{v_0 − V[b_act + β b_loc(ρ) + 4D_G log(16/ρ)]}` (11:795–804). Dividing the absolute bound for the numerator by this gives the per-site normalization cost `q = 2b_act + κ + β b_loc(ρ) + 4D_G log(16/ρ)` of (ch11:replicated-bound), 11:806–813; with `ρ = β̂_i^{-1/2}` this is `q_i^site ≤ C_{J(i)}(1 + log β̂_i)` (13sb:27–39), the bound quoted at 10:171–174. "Normalization" refers to the denominator `Z`; the argument is not the chessboard estimate, which is applied afterwards (11:816–821).
  *Basis:* R (11:795–813; 13sb:27–39). *Where:* 10:172–173 (now with the reference); 13sb:36–37 ("The lower bound for the partition function of Section ch11:replicated therefore adds only …"). *Adopted:* *the lower bound on the partition function by restriction to a ball of small links*, with (ch11:replicated-bound) cited at 10:173 and the stopping scale of Section (ch13:sharp-section) at 10:175.
  *Source:* Scott part2/E-section.tex:26–42 (Lemma "Normalization cost"): "Restrict the denominator to links of chord at most `ĝ_m/4`. There are no flags there, the forced sum is one … The elementary Haar-ball bound gives this set measure at least `(ĝ_m/16)^{4Vν_G^mat}`"; "The per-site exponent `q_m = O(1 + log β̂_m)` comes from the Haar-ball loss `ĝ_m^{−ν_G^mat}` on every link."
*Across chapters:* used in chapter 10 before it is carried out in chapters 11 and 13; since 25 November 2026 10:172–175 describes it and cites the chapter 11 bound and the chapter 13 section. No Lean declaration was searched for.
*See also:* lower bound on the partition function; sparse stopping scale; replication costs.
